explanations.answer: He's deeply disturbed in his spirit
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says he was “…deeply disturbed in his spirit to see that the city was full of idols.” That's no polite frown. Something in him is stirred up, and as we'll see, it gets him talking.

explanations.answer: He's impressed by all the artwork
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but the text doesn't say Paul is admiring any artwork. It says he was “…deeply disturbed in his spirit to see that the city was full of idols.” Disturbed is the word the text gives us. That's the answer.

explanations.answer: He's happy to just go sightseeing
explanations.explanation: Paul isn't described as sightseeing. The text says he was “…deeply disturbed in his spirit…” to see that the city was full of idols. I think a man who's that stirred up has something on his heart. That's the answer.

Not quite, friend. Paul doesn't sit on his hands while he waits. The text says he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and God-fearing Gentiles. He also talked in the marketplace with those he met each day. Quiet is not in his schedule.

Right, it's false. Paul doesn't keep quiet in Athens. He reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and God-fearing Gentiles. He also reasoned in the marketplace with those he met each day. I think Silas and Timothy had no idea what they'd find when they got there!

That's it. Besides the synagogue, Paul reasoned “…in the marketplace with those he met each day.” So his talking wasn't limited to one building. Every day he's out there, meeting people and reasoning with them.

The text doesn't mention a city gate here. It says Paul reasoned in the synagogue, and in the marketplace with those he met each day. I know a gate sounds official, but the marketplace is the answer. It's the other place he talks with people daily.

No riverside in this passage, friend. The text says Paul reasoned in the synagogue, and in the marketplace with those he met each day. Every day! That's a lot of showing up. I once lay in a junk drawer for years and my daily schedule was dust, so I'm impressed. The marketplace is the answer, because that's where the people were.

explanations.answer: He's proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says they said this “…because Paul was proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection.” Some of them said he seemed to be advocating foreign gods. That's the reason the text gives.

explanations.answer: He's carrying little idols from his own homeland
explanations.explanation: The text never says Paul carries a single idol. It tells us why they said it: he was proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection. In fact, the idols are what bother him. He's walking around Athens in the opposite mood.

explanations.answer: He's preaching to them in a language they don't know
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says Paul is speaking in a language they don't know. They even ask him what his new teaching is and say they want to know what it means. The writer tells us the reason for their remark: Paul was proclaiming the good news of Jesus and the resurrection. That's the answer.

Correct. They ask, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?” They add that he's bringing some strange notions to their ears, and they want to know what they mean. I think that's a pretty polite way to say "Okay, explain yourself."

It's actually true. At the Areopagus they ask, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?” They also say they want to know what his strange notions mean. So Paul gets the invitation, and he's about to use it.

explanations.answer: Hearing and talking about new ideas
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The writer says they spent their time “…doing nothing more than hearing and articulating new ideas.” Talking and listening, that's their whole schedule. If you ask me, that's a lot of ideas and a lot of ears.

explanations.answer: Building new temples for their gods
explanations.explanation: The writer doesn't say that. The note says all the Athenians and foreigners spent their time “…doing nothing more than hearing and articulating new ideas.” It's talking, not construction. No hard hats required.

No armies show up in this passage. The writer says the people spent their time “…doing nothing more than hearing and articulating new ideas.” Their favorite sport is conversation. The only thing getting a workout is their ears.

explanations.answer: He's the God Paul now proclaims to them
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says, “Therefore what you worship as something unknown, I now proclaim to you.” They have an altar to an unknown God, and Paul says he's here to tell them about Him. The mystery has an answer.

explanations.answer: He's too far away for anyone to know
explanations.explanation: Paul says nearly the opposite. He says God “…is not far from each one of us.” (Acts 17:27). And he tells them what they worship as unknown, he now proclaims to them. This God can be known.

explanations.answer: He's just one god among their many
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't put Him on the shelf with the others. He says this is the God who made the world and everything in it, the Lord of heaven and earth. So this isn't one more statue in the lineup. And Paul says he now proclaims Him to them.

Not what Paul says. He says the God who made the world is the Lord of heaven and earth and “…does not live in temples made by human hands.” So the answer is False. The temples in Athens aren't where this God lives.

Right, it's false. Paul says the God who made the world is the Lord of heaven and earth and “…does not live in temples made by human hands.” I think that would've been a surprise to a city full of temples. And Paul says it right there in front of them.

explanations.answer: He gives everyone life and breath and everything else
explanations.explanation: Exactly. Paul says God isn't served by human hands as if He needed anything, “…because He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.” We're not handing Him something He lacks. Everything we have comes from Him in the first place.

explanations.answer: He would rather be left alone by the people He made
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that at all. His reason is that God “…Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.” He's the giver, not the one who needs. And Paul goes on to say God is not far from each one of us (Acts 17:27).

explanations.answer: He only accepts service from His priests in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Paul never mentions priests or Jerusalem in this speech. His reason is that God “…Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything else.” That's why He doesn't need anything from human hands. Notice he's speaking to people in Athens, and the point is for everyone.

That's right. Paul says God made every nation of men and “…determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands.” So the times and the places are in His hands. Nobody's nation is an accident to Him.

Actually it's true. Paul says that from one man God made every nation of men. Then he says God “…determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands.” Times and borders are both in the picture.
Yes, seek. Paul says God intended that they “…would seek Him and perhaps reach out for Him and find Him…” Then he adds that God is not far from each one of us. So the search isn't a wild goose chase.
Good guess, but Paul's word here is seek. He says God intended that they “…would seek Him and perhaps reach out for Him and find Him…” It's about looking and reaching out. And Paul says He's not far.

Praise is a fine thing to do, but it's not the word in this verse. Paul says God intended that they “…would seek Him and perhaps reach out for Him and find Him…” The word is seek. It's like looking for your keys, except the One you're looking for is close by.
Paul says the opposite. He says God “…is not far from each one of us.” God is close. And Paul goes on to say that in Him we live and move and have our being.
Correct, it's false. Paul says God “…is not far from each one of us.” He's near, not distant. That's good news for anyone who's been looking.

explanations.answer: An image of gold or silver or stone
explanations.explanation: You got it. Paul says we should not think the Divine Being is “…like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by man’s skill and imagination.” We're God's offspring, so thinking He's a statue makes no sense. It's a serious point, and he makes it plainly.

explanations.answer: The sun and the moon above
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention the sun or the moon here. He says we shouldn't think the Divine Being is like “…gold or silver or stone, an image formed by man’s skill and imagination.” His point is about things people make. The lights in the sky aren't in this sentence.

explanations.answer: The great sea and its waves
explanations.explanation: The sea doesn't come up in this speech. Paul says we should not think the Divine Being is like “…gold or silver or stone, an image formed by man’s skill and imagination.” He's talking about images people shape by hand. No waves in this verse.

That's the word. Paul says God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times, but He “…now commands all people everywhere to repent.” Notice the word everywhere. That's not just for Athens or one crowd. It's for every person.

Rest sounds nice, but that's not the command. Paul says God “…now commands all people everywhere to repent.” To repent is to turn around and change direction. And the command goes to all people everywhere, not just the folks in front of Paul.
Paul doesn't say sacrifice here. He says God “…now commands all people everywhere to repent.” That's the word in this verse. It's a call to turn, and it goes to everyone.
Yes. Paul says God “…has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed.” The day is set and the judge is appointed. That's why Paul says repent.

Paul says nothing about rebuilding temples. In fact, he's already said God does not live in temples made by human hands. What he says about that day is that God “…will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed.” That's the answer.

Wars don't come up in this speech, friend. Paul says God has set a day when He “…will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed.” So the day is about justice, and the Man He appointed is the one doing the judging. Then Paul backs it up: God “…has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead.” That's why he tells them to repent in verse 30.

explanations.answer: By raising Him from the dead
explanations.explanation: Right on. Paul says God “…has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead.” The proof is something God did. He raised the Man He appointed.

explanations.answer: By sending signs in the sky
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention any signs in the sky. He says God “…has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead.” The proof is the raising from the dead. That's the answer.

explanations.answer: By writing it on stone tablets
explanations.explanation: No tablets in this speech. Paul says God “…has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead.” That's the proof. I'd say it's a bigger deal than any carving.
That's it. When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, “…some began to mock him…” The text says some, not everyone. And right after that, we hear from others who respond differently.
The text doesn't say that. It says that when they heard about the resurrection of the dead, “…some began to mock him…” Mocking, not jail. And then Paul simply leaves the Areopagus.

explanations.answer: Drag him out to stone him
explanations.explanation: That's not in this scene. The text says that when they heard about the resurrection of the dead, “…some began to mock him…” No rocks, just mockery. Others in the crowd want to hear more, which is a very different reaction.
Yes. Others said, “We want to hear you again on this topic.” So the same speech gets two reactions, mocking from some and interest from others. Same sermon, different ears.
Actually it's true. Alongside the ones who mock, others said, “We want to hear you again on this topic.” So they're not finished with the conversation. The same speech gets two different reactions.

Yes, Damaris. The text says some joined Paul and believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite, “…a woman named Damaris, and others who were with them.” Think about that room, friend. Some of the crowd had just mocked Paul, and she heard the very same sermon and believed. Her name made it into the Bible, and I'd say that's a pretty good place to end up.

Lydia is a real woman in Paul's journey, a dealer in purple cloth (Acts 16:14), but she's not in this scene. Here the text names “…a woman named Damaris…” Different city, different story. Easy to mix up when there's a lot of names.

Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea (Romans 16:1), is not in this passage. The text says the woman who believed in Athens is “…a woman named Damaris…” Phoebe shows up later in a letter. Right name for a different place.
